questions.question: How do you use verify() in Mockito to check method interactions?
questions.title: Mockito verify() Method | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`verify(mock).method(args)`** asserts that `method(args)` was called exactly once on the mock. If not called, or called with different args, the test fails. This is behavior verification — checking that your code interacted with dependencies correctly.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verify() to check return values instead of assertions on the actual result — verify checks that a method was called, not what it returned
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between state verification (assertions on results) and behavior verification (verify on interactions)

sections.title: Verify Interactions Were Made
sections.content: `verify(emailService).sendConfirmation(expectedOrder)` — asserts that `sendConfirmation` was called exactly once with `expectedOrder`. **Default**: once. `verify(mock, times(2)).method()` — called exactly 2 times. `verify(mock, never()).method()` — never called. **When to verify vs assert**: verify interactions that are side effects (send email, save to DB) where the return value isn't the test's focus.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- verify(mock): exactly once (default)
- verify(mock, times(n)): exactly n times
- verify(mock, never()): never called
- verify(mock, atLeast(n)): at least n times
- verify(mock, atLeastOnce()): at least once
- verify(mock, atMost(n)): at most n times
- verify with argument matchers: any(), eq(), specific values
- Don't verify return values — use assertions for that

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: verify checks that a method was called on a mock with specific arguments. By default verify asserts the method was called exactly once. I use it for verifying side effects — if OrderService should save the order and send a confirmation email, I verify that both repository.save and emailService.sendConfirmation were called. I use times(n) when a method should be called a specific number of times, and never() when I want to assert it wasn't called at all. The key distinction is that verify checks interactions, not return values — I use assertions like assertEquals for return values.

questions.question: What is ArgumentCaptor in Mockito and how do you use it?
questions.title: Mockito ArgumentCaptor | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **ArgumentCaptor captures the argument that was passed to a mock method** so you can assert on it. Use it when the argument is constructed inside the method under test and you can't compare it directly — like a dynamically created object passed to `save()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Advanced Mockito usage — very common in Spring service tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using eq() or any() when you actually need to inspect the argument — ArgumentCaptor gives you the real object
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the full pattern: @Captor annotation, verify with capture, then getValue() assertion

sections.title: Capture and Inspect Arguments
sections.content: `@Captor ArgumentCaptor<Order> orderCaptor;` in test class. In test: `verify(orderRepository).save(orderCaptor.capture())`. Then: `Order saved = orderCaptor.getValue()`. Assert: `assertEquals("PENDING", saved.getStatus())`. Use case: `OrderService.createOrder()` builds an Order object internally, sets its status, then calls repository.save. You can't pass this order from outside — use ArgumentCaptor to capture what was actually passed to save.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @Captor annotation or ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Type.class)
- verify(mock).method(captor.capture()): captures the arg
- captor.getValue(): get the captured argument
- captor.getAllValues(): for multiple invocations
- Use when: object is created internally and you need to verify its state
- Alternative: custom matcher if the assertion is reusable
- ArgumentCaptor is for verify — not for when() stubbing
- @Captor requires @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to activate

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ArgumentCaptor captures the actual argument that was passed to a mock method so I can assert on its properties. I declare a @Captor field of the appropriate type in my test class. In the verify call I use captor.capture() instead of any() or a specific value. After verify, captor.getValue() gives me the actual object that was passed. A typical use case is testing that when a service creates an Order and saves it, the saved order has the correct status and customer ID set. I can't pass that order from outside the service — it's constructed internally — so I capture it from the repository.save call.

questions.question: What is verifyNoMoreInteractions() and when should you use it?
questions.title: Mockito verifyNoMoreInteractions | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock)`** fails if any method was called that wasn't already verified. Use it to ensure a mock wasn't called unexpectedly. However, overuse makes tests brittle — prefer `verify(mock, never()).specificMethod()` for targeted negative assertions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding of when to use comprehensive vs targeted verification
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding verifyNoMoreInteractions on every mock — makes tests overly strict and brittle to refactoring
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the tradeoff: comprehensive verification vs test brittleness

sections.title: Ensure No Unexpected Calls
sections.content: `verifyNoMoreInteractions(emailService)` — if any method on `emailService` was called that wasn't covered by a preceding `verify()`, the test fails. Useful for: security-sensitive code where extra calls are errors, strict protocol adherence. **Risk**: a valid refactoring that adds a new interaction (e.g., adding a logging call) will break the test even though behavior is correct. Prefer `verify(mock, never()).dangerousMethod()` for specific negations.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock1, mock2, ...): can accept multiple mocks
- Fails if: any interaction not covered by preceding verify()
- verifyNoInteractions(mock): no interactions at all (no preceding verify needed)
- Brittle: breaks on valid refactoring that adds logging, metrics, etc.
- Use sparingly: security-critical, financial transactions
- Prefer: verify(mock, never()).specificMethod() for targeted negation
- Mockito 2: ignoreStubs() wraps mocks to ignore stubbed methods

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: verifyNoMoreInteractions ensures that after all my explicit verify calls, no other method was called on the mock. It's useful when I want to guarantee that a sensitive service — like a payment gateway — wasn't called in scenarios where it shouldn't be. The downside is that it makes tests brittle: if someone adds a legitimate logging call or metrics call on that mock, the test breaks even though the behavior is correct. I use it selectively for security or financial critical code, and prefer the more targeted approach of verify-never on a specific method when I just want to assert one thing wasn't called.

questions.question: How do you verify the order of method calls in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito InOrder Verification | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use `InOrder` to verify methods were called in a specific sequence.** `InOrder inOrder = inOrder(mock1, mock2); inOrder.verify(mock1).methodA(); inOrder.verify(mock2).methodB()`. The test fails if methodB was called before methodA.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of InOrder verification for protocol-sensitive code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using regular verify() and assuming order is checked — regular verify doesn't care about order
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete scenario where order matters: begin transaction → process → commit, or validate → save → notify

sections.title: Sequence-Sensitive Verification
sections.content: `InOrder inOrder = inOrder(transactionManager, orderRepository)`. Then: `inOrder.verify(transactionManager).begin()`, `inOrder.verify(orderRepository).save(any())`, `inOrder.verify(transactionManager).commit()`. If `save()` is called before `begin()`, or `commit()` before `save()`, the test fails. Regular `verify()` calls don't enforce order.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- inOrder(mock1, mock2): create InOrder with the mocks to verify
- inOrder.verify(mock).method(): verify in expected sequence
- Regular verify(): order doesn't matter
- Can include multiple mocks in one InOrder
- InOrder doesn't require verifying ALL interactions — only the declared order
- Use case: begin/process/commit, validate/save/notify
- Over-specifying order = brittle tests
- Only use when order genuinely matters for correctness

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To verify the order of method calls I use Mockito's InOrder. I create an InOrder object passing all the mocks whose interaction order I care about. Then I call inOrder.verify instead of regular verify. The test fails if the actual call order doesn't match the verification order. A classic example is a transactional workflow: I want to verify begin transaction is called before save, and save is called before commit. Regular verify calls don't enforce order — InOrder is specifically for this. I use it sparingly because over-specifying order makes tests brittle.

questions.question: How do you verify that a method was never called in Mockito?
questions.title: Verifying a Method Was Never Called
questions.direct_answer: Use verify(mock, never()).method() to assert a method was never invoked, or verifyNoInteractions(mock) to assert no methods on the mock were called at all.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the VerificationMode options beyond the default times(1)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not verifying negative cases — assuming the absence of a call when you should explicitly assert it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between never(), times(0), verifyNoInteractions(), and verifyNoMoreInteractions() and explain when each is appropriate

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
When you want to assert that a specific method was never called on a mock, you use verify with the never() verification mode: verify(emailService, never()).sendEmail(any()). This is equivalent to verify(emailService, times(0)).sendEmail(any()), but never() communicates the intent more clearly.

This is useful for testing negative paths — for example, verifying that a notification is not sent when an operation fails, or that a repository's save method is not called when validation fails.

For broader assertions there are two more options. verifyNoInteractions(mock) asserts that absolutely no methods were called on a specific mock object during the test. verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock) is different — it asserts that after all your explicit verify() calls, there were no additional unexpected interactions. That one is more dangerous because it can make tests brittle as your implementation evolves, so use it sparingly.

A practical tip: negative verifications should be used intentionally for business-critical cases, not as a habit. Testing that every mock method was not called in every test adds noise without proportional value. Focus on verifying behaviors that represent real business rules.

sections.title: Key Points
content: verify(mock, never()).method() — asserts the specific method was never invoked
verify(mock, times(0)).method() — equivalent but less readable than never()
verifyNoInteractions(mock) — asserts no method on the mock was called at all
verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock) — asserts no unexpected calls after explicit verifications (use sparingly)

questions.question: What is verifyNoMoreInteractions() and when is it useful?
questions.title: verifyNoMoreInteractions() in Mockito
questions.direct_answer: verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock) fails the test if any method was called on the mock that was not covered by a preceding verify() call, ensuring no unexpected interactions occurred.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the purpose and dangers of strict interaction verification
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verifyNoMoreInteractions() in every test, causing tests to fail whenever the implementation changes even when the change is intentional and correct
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast it with verifyNoInteractions() and explain that strict interaction testing trades flexibility for safety in specific high-stakes scenarios

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock) is a strict assertion that says: I have already verified everything I expected this mock to do, and I am asserting that nothing else happened. If any method on the mock was called during the test that you did not explicitly verify, this call will fail the test.

It is useful in scenarios where you want to be absolutely sure about the complete interaction contract — for example, verifying that a billing service was called exactly once and nothing else happened, which is important for financial logic or security-sensitive operations.

However, it comes with a significant downside: it makes tests fragile. If you add a new feature that legitimately calls an additional method on the mock, all tests with verifyNoMoreInteractions() will break even though the behavior is correct. This is why many experienced developers consider it an anti-pattern when used indiscriminately.

A simpler alternative for whole-mock checks is verifyNoInteractions(mock), which simply asserts that the mock was not touched at all — useful when you want to confirm a code path completely skipped a dependency.

The recommendation: use verifyNoMoreInteractions() only in high-stakes, narrow tests where the exact interaction contract is a critical business requirement, not as a default in every test.

sections.title: Key Points
content: verifyNoMoreInteractions() fails if any unverified interaction occurred on the mock
Must be called after all explicit verify() calls to be meaningful
Can make tests brittle — fails on any legitimate new interaction added to the implementation
verifyNoInteractions() is simpler: asserts the mock was not called at all

questions.question: What is the difference between verify(mock, times(n)), atLeast(n), and atMost(n) in Mockito?
questions.title: Verify Invocation Count Modes
questions.direct_answer: times(n) asserts exactly n calls; atLeast(n) asserts at least n calls; atMost(n) asserts no more than n calls — all are passed as the second argument to verify().

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verify(mock) without a count argument and assuming it checks for exactly one call — which is actually what it does, but candidates often don't know the default is times(1)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that over-specifying call counts makes tests brittle and suggest only verifying counts when the count itself is business-critical

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Mockito's verify() method accepts an optional VerificationMode as its second argument that controls how many times a method must have been called. The modes are: times(n) — exactly n invocations; atLeast(n) — n or more invocations; atMost(n) — n or fewer invocations; never() — zero invocations; atLeastOnce() — one or more invocations.

When you write verify(mock).someMethod() without any mode, Mockito uses times(1) as the default — it asserts the method was called exactly once.

The modes are useful for different scenarios. times(1) is appropriate when you need to ensure no duplicate calls, for example verifying that a costly external API was called exactly once and not re-tried unnecessarily. atLeastOnce() is useful in loops where the exact count depends on input size but you need at least one call. never() is important for negative assertions — confirming that a method was not called when a condition was false.

A word of caution: over-specifying invocation counts can make your tests brittle. If you assert verify(mock, times(3)) and an internal refactoring reduces the calls to two (while the external behaviour stays identical), your test breaks for the wrong reason. Reserve count verification for cases where the count is genuinely part of the contract — like 'charge the card exactly once' or 'send the notification no more than once'.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Default verify(mock) is equivalent to verify(mock, times(1)).
atLeast(n), atMost(n), never(), atLeastOnce() cover flexible count assertions.
Only verify counts when the count is part of the business contract.
Over-counting assertions make tests fragile under refactoring.

questions.question: How do you use ArgumentCaptor to assert on complex objects passed to a mock?
questions.title: ArgumentCaptor for Complex Assertions
questions.direct_answer: Declare an ArgumentCaptor for the type, pass captor.capture() to verify(), then call captor.getValue() to retrieve and assert on the captured argument.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to write detailed assertions on method arguments in Mockito
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using argument matchers like any() when you actually need to inspect what was passed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete example involving a DTO or entity and assert on individual fields of the captured value

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Sometimes you need to verify not just that a method was called, but what object was passed to it. If the object is complex — like an Order entity created inside the method — you cannot easily construct the exact same instance for comparison. ArgumentCaptor solves this.

You create a captor with ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class) or with @Captor annotation. Then in your verify call you use captor.capture() as the argument matcher: verify(orderRepository).save(captor.capture()). After verify() runs, the captured value is available via captor.getValue(). If the method was called multiple times, captor.getAllValues() returns a list.

Here is a concrete example. Suppose you are testing an OrderService.placeOrder() method that creates an Order internally and saves it. You cannot compare the saved Order with == because you don't have a reference to it. With ArgumentCaptor you write: verify(orderRepository).save(captor.capture()); Order saved = captor.getValue(); assertEquals("PENDING", saved.getStatus()); assertEquals(customerId, saved.getCustomerId()). This gives you field-level assertions on the captured object.

ArgumentCaptor is more readable than a custom argThat() matcher when you have multiple fields to check, and it gives better failure messages because the assertion is on the individual field. Use it whenever the argument to a mock is constructed inside the method under test and you need to validate its content.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Pass captor.capture() inside verify() to record the argument.
Use captor.getValue() for one call, captor.getAllValues() for multiple calls.
Ideal for objects created inside the method under test where you need field-level assertions.
